title: Why we’re building Jago
description: The experiences behind Jago: starting with shops’ needs, finding suppliers and supporting wholesale orders of African products.
paragraphs: We’re building DEMAA, a venture studio. Jago is one of the ventures we’re developing, drawing on our experience with African products.
The first venture that really brought us face to face with the challenges of bringing African products to market was Madame Karité, a shea butter brand.

We thought the hardest part would be the brand and packaging. In practice, everything around the product took the most time: finding the right suppliers, managing quality and transport, and finding buyers.

I then spent a year in Mali. We launched a range of frozen vegetables, cut and ready to cook. We had secured listings with two retailers when the energy crisis hit. Power cuts meant we could no longer reliably maintain the cold chain. For frozen food, that was a fundamental obstacle, and the venture stopped there.
The product was good and we had places to sell it. But just one link in the chain failing can bring everything else to a halt.

We later launched an herbal tea brand, still running today, with some production and packaging done locally. Once again, we had many things to manage at the same time: suppliers, packaging, machinery, quality, transport and buyers.
Each problem can be solved on its own. When you launch a brand, though, you often have to solve them all at once.
These experiences changed how we thought about the problem.
We began asking how we could make this chain easier for shops looking for African products in bulk, and for the suppliers who want to sell them.
That’s where Jago began.

Today, Jago starts with requests from shops, grocers, resellers and online retailers looking for African products in bulk. We gather their requirements, then look for suitable products within our supplier network.
Jago manages the relationship between customer and supplier, with agreed prices and support from the initial request through to the order.
What we want to test is whether this support makes sourcing easy enough for customers to come back when they need something else.

The business model still needs to be validated. Our starting hypothesis is a subscription for sellers or suppliers. We’re taking the time to find the right pricing and terms, informed by requests and our first conversations.
After several ventures where we had to manage much of this chain ourselves, we want to make that work easier for others. That’s what we’re building with Jago.

title: How we’re building Jago’s go-to-market strategy
description: Starting with shops’ wholesale needs, finding suitable suppliers and managing the relationship: Jago’s go-to-market strategy.
paragraphs: At first, we mainly imagined Jago as a platform to help African brands sell wholesale.
Conversations with shops and partners changed our understanding: the immediate need is about finding the products people want and the right suppliers to provide them.
So we’re building Jago around demand.
These conversations help us understand which products shops are actually looking for. Those needs guide the development of our supplier network and the tools that support the service.
We use our APOP method: Audience, Positioning, Offer, Promotion.
Audience
We’re focusing on shops, grocers, resellers and online retailers looking for African products in bulk.
We want to test a need they may share: finding suitable products, reliable suppliers and clear terms takes time and often depends on personal networks.
We want to understand what each business needs, what it already buys and how often, before focusing our efforts on the most recurring requests.
We compare the needs of different shops: product categories, volumes, frequency and the difficulties they face. This helps us identify the groups for whom Jago could be most useful.
Positioning
**For shops looking for African products in bulk, Jago finds suitable suppliers and manages the commercial relationship, with agreed prices and order follow-up.**
The customer sends their request to Jago. We find a relevant offer within our supplier network and remain their point of contact as the order progresses.

Today, this search often involves personal networks, trade shows, WhatsApp and several conversations with suppliers. Jago brings the sourcing work and commercial follow-up together through one point of contact who understands the request.
Payment, transport, import and delivery terms need to be clarified for each order. The responsibilities of Jago and its partners still need to be tested in the first trials.
Offer
The first version starts with a request, rather than a catalogue we need to fill.

- Gather the requirements: products, quantities and purchase frequency.
- Find a suitable offer from our suppliers.
- Present products, prices and terms clearly.
- Manage the supplier relationship and follow the order through.
Some of this work can remain manual at first. It lets us understand the requests before building more tools.
We’re also taking the time to test the business model, prices and terms.
Our starting hypothesis is a subscription for sellers or suppliers. We’re taking the time to find the right pricing and terms through requests and early conversations.
Promotion
We’re starting with our network of shops and grocers, introductions and partnerships with retail networks.
The aim is to speak with shops, gather their requirements and see which requests we can actually fulfil.
What we want to test
Do requests turn into orders, and do customers come back to source products again?
We also track the products requested, the requests we can fulfil and the issues that slow orders down. We compare these signals across types of shop to decide where to focus our efforts.

title: Jago’s action plan
description: Shop networks, specific requests, clear offers and order follow-up: Jago’s action plan.
paragraphs: Once we’ve set the strategy, we move on to the action plan.
We keep the same structure: Attract, Convert, Retain, with Nurturing and Referrals running across all three.
Attract
We start with conversations with shops, grocers, resellers and online retailers who buy, or want to buy, African products in bulk.
We draw on our network of shop owners, introductions and partnerships with shop and grocery networks. We record each request: product, quantity, frequency, destination and sourcing difficulties.
We’re mainly looking for recurring requests we can respond to usefully.
Convert
For Jago, conversion doesn’t necessarily mean taking payment straight away.
The first step is a specific request we can answer with clear products, prices and terms.
We find suitable suppliers in our network and manage the relationship between the two parties. Jago remains the point of contact to move the request forward and follow the order through.
We look at whether the offers meet the need and lead to orders.
Retain
The most interesting signal is a customer coming back.
Do they return for another product or to replenish their stock?
We confirm the stages of the order, answer questions and follow problems through to resolution. After delivery, we gather feedback on the products and plan the next replenishment with the customer.
Product quality, clear terms and the quality of our follow-up all matter to this relationship. Feedback helps us understand what makes customers want to order again.
Nurturing
Not every shop has an immediate need.
We can stay useful with content that helps them source products, identify suitable options and understand what’s available.
This content supports their needs over time. It isn’t our main acquisition channel at the start.
With suppliers, we stay in touch around real requests, without promising volumes we don’t yet have.
Referrals
One shop may introduce us to another. A supplier may point us towards a producer or a complementary product.
These introductions are part of the work on the ground, even before a first order.
We focus on qualified requests, orders and returning customers.
Metrics to track
Qualified requests, offers presented, orders and replenishment frequency, by type of shop.

title: Why we’re building Dumaan
description: “What’s for dinner?” Dumaan starts with family life and the most time-consuming West African food preparations to make meals easier.
paragraphs: “Mum, what’s for dinner?”
When you work, have children or simply have busy days, that question comes around quickly. You may want to eat the dishes you grew up with without having several hours to prepare them.
My mother has always found ways to save time: preparing things ahead, freezing them and getting the longest steps out of the way.
That’s the thinking behind Dumaan.
What can we prepare in advance to make the meal easier, while keeping the flavours and the pleasure of cooking?
At first, we thought about restaurants and caterers, because some preparations take up a lot of their time.

As we explored the idea, though, we became more interested in everyday family life. Coming home from work, deciding what to eat and starting every preparation from scratch: that’s the problem we want to tackle first.
We’re starting by exploring the needs of families who want to cook West African food more easily.
Ready-to-cook pastels, chopped vegetables and pre-prepared dish bases are some of the options. The exact products, formats and prices still need to be refined through the first tests.
For pastels, you have to make the dough, prepare the filling and shape each piece. Having those steps already done makes a tangible difference to the time needed to prepare a meal.
We’re looking for preparations that save enough time to become part of people’s regular routines.
We’ll also test some preparations with restaurants and caterers to compare their needs and uses.
To begin with, we’ll look at what families buy, how they use it and what they buy again. That will tell us where Dumaan really makes everyday life easier.

title: How we’re building Dumaan’s go-to-market strategy
description: Dumaan’s strategy: start with families, test preparations that make meals easier and observe repeat purchases.
paragraphs: Dumaan starts with an everyday problem: wanting to cook West African dishes when there isn’t enough time for the longest preparation steps.
We use the same APOP method: Audience, Positioning, Offer, Promotion.
Audience
Families and busy working people who want to enjoy these dishes at home with less preparation are our initial hypothesis.
The question is practical: “What’s for dinner?” You need an idea, the ingredients and time to cook, often after an already busy day.
We want to understand which steps take the most time and what families would be willing to buy to make them easier.
Positioning
**Dumaan offers frozen West African food products that take care of some of the most time-consuming preparation, making it easier to cook at home.**
The idea is to make the meal easier while leaving families free to finish it in their own way.
Offer
We’re starting with a few products whose time-saving benefit is easy to understand.
Ready-to-cook pastels, chopped vegetables and some dish bases are options to test. The range, formats and prices still need to be refined.
We want to see what genuinely fits into families’ habits.
We test portion sizes, freezer space, preparation steps at home and acceptable prices. These details determine whether a product fits easily into a family meal.
Promotion
We’re testing a signature “What’s for dinner?” video promoted through advertising, alongside tastings and local word of mouth.
We adjust the messages and budget based on the first enquiries and orders.
Families remain the priority. We’re also testing some preparations with restaurants and caterers to compare their needs and uses.
What we want to test
Which products meet a regular need for families and food businesses, enough to be used and bought again?

title: Dumaan’s action plan
description: Tastings, first purchases, meal ideas and repeat orders: Dumaan’s action plan to test its value for families.
paragraphs: Dumaan’s first action plan focuses on families. Testing some preparations with restaurants and caterers will also help us compare needs and uses.
We keep the same structure: Attract, Convert, Retain, with Nurturing and Referrals running across all three.
Attract
We want to speak to families about everyday life: “What’s for dinner?”, the time they have and the preparations they put off because they take too long.

We create a signature video around “What’s for dinner?”, showing a real meal being prepared. We promote it through advertising from the start, supported by tastings and local introductions to families.
We track enquiries and first orders to refine the messages and budget.
Convert
We offer a few products that are easy to understand and try.
The format, price and instructions should make it immediately clear how to use them at home.
The first orders will also help us refine the range, quantities and delivery arrangements.
Retain
A first order may come from curiosity. Repeat purchases will tell us more about the product’s place in everyday life.

We support first use with clear storage and preparation instructions. We answer questions, ask for feedback after meals and make reordering easy. We track repeat purchases, taste, portions and time saved.
Nurturing
We stay useful between purchases with meal ideas, preparation tips and information about available products.
The content should help people answer the dinner question, rather than simply remind them to buy.
Referrals
A happy family may introduce Dumaan to people they know.
We’ll look at whether these recommendations lead to new trials and then new purchases.
Feedback on the first meals and repeat orders will guide the next formats and products.
Metrics to track
First orders, products used, repeat purchases and order frequency, by customer type.

title: Why we’re building Tiimora
description: From working with accounting firms to the first pilots: why Tiimora focuses on client requests and deadlines.
paragraphs: Tiimora grew directly out of our work with accounting firms.
We help them with business structure, processes and organisation. We soon realised that much of their daily workload came from everything around the accounting work, as well as the accounting itself.
Asking clients for the right information, collecting documents, sending reminders, tracking deadlines, assigning tasks, checking what’s been done and making sure nothing is forgotten.
One reminder doesn’t amount to much. Repeated across dozens or hundreds of client files, it takes a lot of time and, above all, a lot of mental space.

Before considering building software, we started putting systems together with Airtable, Fillout, Make and other tools. We automated some reminders, created forms, centralised information and tried to avoid everything depending on one person’s memory.
The same needs kept coming up across different firms.
Meanwhile, accounting software has evolved considerably. Solutions such as Pennylane handle much of the core accounting work very well, but that doesn’t remove everything that happens around it.
A firm can have excellent accounting software and still manage reminders, some client requests, tasks and processes across email, spreadsheets, calendars, WhatsApp and staff members’ memories.
That’s the space Tiimora aims to cover.
We’re deliberately starting with a fairly focused scope: client requests and deadlines.
The initial promise is simple: fewer manual reminders, less to keep in your head and a clearer view of what needs to be done.
Two firms are currently piloting Tiimora. They help us see what gets used, what removes work and what, by contrast, doesn’t add enough value.
The vision may grow broader over time. We can already see how much a tool like this could cover across a firm’s operations.
But we’d rather build around real use than a long list of features decided in advance.

title: How we’re building Tiimora’s go-to-market strategy
description: Audience, positioning, a test offer and channels: Tiimora’s go-to-market strategy for accounting firms with 3 to 20 employees.
paragraphs: Tiimora starts in a market we already know well: accounting firms.
We use the same APOP method: Audience, Positioning, Offer, Promotion.
Audience
Who do we want to serve?
Accounting firms with 3 to 20 employees.

The problem we want to solve is tangible: even with good accounting software, some of the work around it remains manual or scattered across tools, including client reminders, information requests, documents, deadlines and tasks to follow up.
On their own, these aren’t major problems. Repeated across dozens or hundreds of client files, they take time and create mental load.
Two pilot firms are already testing Tiimora, allowing us to compare this hypothesis with real use.
Positioning
Tiimora helps accounting firms with 3 to 20 employees track client requests, documents and deadlines in one place, alongside their existing accounting tools.
It centralises operational follow-up and automates some reminders, complementing Pennylane, Silae and other specialist tools.
The initial promise is simple: fewer manual reminders, less to keep in your head and better visibility.
Offer
What are we offering today?
The current test price is €199 per month.
We’re considering a setup fee, but the amount still needs to be tested.
The first version focuses mainly on client requests and deadlines.
Other features may follow, but we don’t want to sell a complete suite before validating this first use case.
Promotion
How will we reach this audience?
Our three priority channels are:

- Useful LinkedIn content on client requests, missing documents and responsibilities.
- LinkedIn advertising to distribute these resources from the start.
- Introductions and partnerships with organisational consultants, trainers and accounting firm networks.
A practical resource opens the conversation. We then offer a process review or a demo tailored to the firm’s needs.
The two pilot firms should also help us produce concrete case studies if the results are strong enough.
What we want to test
What we want to observe:

- Does the problem actually lead to a purchase decision?
- Do firms adopt Tiimora in their daily work?
- Does the product genuinely remove manual work?
- Which uses become recurring?
- What level of pricing and support is acceptable?
These signals will guide how we expand the product and its go-to-market strategy.

title: Tiimora’s action plan
description: Demos, onboarding and recurring use: Tiimora’s action plan to acquire and retain its first accounting firms.
paragraphs: Once the strategy is set, the action plan is fairly straightforward.
We keep the same structure: Attract, Convert, Retain, with Nurturing and Referrals running across all three.
Attract
We want to speak directly to firms with 3 to 20 employees about problems they recognise immediately: client reminders, information requests, deadlines and organisation.

We start with LinkedIn content showing exactly how to organise client requests, track missing documents and clarify responsibilities in an accounting firm. We share the method and an example of how it works in Tiimora.

We amplify this content through LinkedIn advertising from the start. Alongside that, we ask for introductions and build partnerships with consultants who help organise accounting firms, trainers and accounting firm networks.
A process map or a request-tracking template helps us understand the firm’s needs and start a useful relationship.
Convert
Conversion needs to start with how the firm actually works.
We offer a 30-minute process review, followed by a demo focused on the problem identified: a client request, a reminder, a deadline or a simple workflow.
The test price is €199 per month.
We’re considering a setup fee, but the amount still needs to be validated.
We make the scope of the offer and next steps clear. Setup is supported to help the firm get started with its first process.
Retain

After setup, we guide onboarding, help configure a first process and answer the team’s questions. A follow-up session helps remove obstacles, check that the firm is getting value and gradually expand usage.
Is the team using Tiimora for recurring tasks?
Are there fewer manual reminders, fewer things to keep in mind and a clearer view of what needs to be done?
We mainly want to measure actual use and perceived value, rather than just login numbers.
Nurturing
Not every firm will be ready at the same time.
We send content and resources related to the need they’ve described: process examples, tracking templates and use cases. Our conversations help answer questions and maintain a good relationship.
The aim is to stay useful until the problem becomes a priority.
Referrals
Trust matters a great deal in this market.
A pilot firm, a satisfied client or a trusted partner can make an introduction that carries far more weight than a cold message.
So we want to take every good interaction seriously, even when it doesn’t immediately lead to a sale.
We track the journey from resources to the process review, then setup, and regular use of the first process. Feedback from firms helps us refine the support and choose which uses to develop next.
Metrics to track
Requests for a process review or demo, setups completed, regular use of the first process and time spent on reminders.

title: Why we’re building DEMAA
description: Why DEMAA shares resources to test opportunities, build profitable businesses and invest with discipline.
paragraphs: DEMAA began with a simple observation: we regularly spot opportunities because we already work within certain markets.
Tiimora grew out of our work with accounting firms.
Jago grew out of several experiences with African products, production and bringing them to market.
Each venture could have been launched as an independent business from day one.
But much of the work repeats: shaping an offer, building a product, creating content, finding the first customers, setting up tools and managing some of the administration or sales.
The idea behind the studio is to share that work.
The aim is to test several opportunities with the same team and method, then gradually focus resources on those showing real signals, rather than launch as many ventures as possible.
We also want to avoid building too much too soon.
A venture can be promising even when its audience, offer or business model isn’t yet clear.
So we start by testing: speaking with the people concerned, putting an initial offer in front of them, observing what they do and deciding whether it deserves more time and capital.
Depending on the venture, that decision may come quickly or take several months.
Profitability also matters a great deal in how we think about the studio.
We don’t aim to build businesses that necessarily depend on successive funding rounds. We want them to become resilient, fund their own operations and create lasting value.
We may hold some for the income they generate. Others may be sold if that makes sense.
We aren’t deciding today how each company will eventually be exited. We want to build businesses that leave us with several options.
The studio shares some strategy, marketing, sales, finance, administration and tools.
When a venture becomes a business in its own right, though, it also needs to build what makes it distinct: its team, sector expertise and operational capabilities.
We’ve also chosen to document some of the work.
We won’t share everything, and the aim isn’t to turn DEMAA into a media business.
We mainly share decisions others might find useful: why we choose an audience, how we approach go-to-market, what we test and what changes our minds.
It also pushes us to be clearer about our own hypotheses.

Ultimately, DEMAA gives structure to something we were already doing in a more scattered way: starting with problems we know, testing with discipline and investing more only when experience on the ground gives us good reasons to do so.
What’s next?
This first series has helped us set out Jago, Tiimora and Dumaan, their go-to-market strategies, their action plans and how we organise the tests behind them.
From here, we’ll mainly focus on building.
Detailed updates will be collected on the DEMAA website: progress, changes, test results and important decisions.
On LinkedIn, we’ll return when there’s something useful to share: a result, a change in our hypothesis, a need, a hire, a partner we’re looking for or a learning worth making public.

title: Our go-to-market system
description: Our go-to-market system: APOP for strategy, Attract, Convert, Retain for action, with Nurturing and Referrals throughout.
paragraphs: As we built several ventures, we needed a common approach to structure decisions without applying the same tactics to every market.
We organised it into two layers: strategy, then the action plan.
1. Strategy: APOP
Audience
Who do we want to serve?
Which groups or segments do we want to test?
What problem does each group face?
If there are several, which seems most important to focus on today, and why?
We don’t want to force a single ideal customer profile too early. For some ventures, the audience is already fairly clear. For others, we compare several groups before choosing.
What we want to clarify is:
**who + a problem important enough to act on.**
Positioning
Once we understand the audience and the problem, we formulate the positioning.
We use a simple structure:
**For [audience] who [problem], [product] is a [category] that [main benefit].**
And, where useful:
**Unlike [alternative], [important difference].**
The alternative isn’t necessarily a direct competitor. It might be the status quo, a manual process, an informal network or several tools used together.
If there are several audiences with different problems, we may need different positioning for each.
The point is to make a clear decision about the customer, the problem, the category and the value we bring, rather than write an elegant sentence.
Offer
What are we offering today to solve this problem?
Product or service, format, price, support, terms, what’s included and what isn’t.
If there are several segments, should the offer be the same for each or adapted?
At first, some of the offer may still be a hypothesis to test.
Promotion
How do we reach each audience?
Which channels best suit each segment?
LinkedIn, targeted outreach, partners, advertising, work on the ground, content and events: the mix depends on the venture.
At this stage, we choose the channels.
What we want to test
After APOP, we add a simple question:
**What do we need to observe to believe this strategy is working?**
It could be a qualified enquiry, an introduction that moves forward, a purchase, a repeat purchase, activation, retention, an accepted price or another sufficiently concrete behaviour.
If there are several segments, we compare the signals across them before deciding where to focus resources.
2. The action plan
The action plan sets out what we’ll actually do within the channels we’ve chosen.
Attract
What actions will help us reach the right people and build trust?
For example: posting on LinkedIn, contacting a specific prospect list, working with partners, organising tastings or launching a targeted campaign.
Convert
How do we turn that interest into a concrete next step?
It could be a demo, an introduction, a trial purchase, a landing page, a tasting or a very clear, simple offer.
Retain
What needs to happen for a customer to stay, buy again or reuse the product?
We look at actual use, experience, repeat purchases, retention and the value delivered.
Two layers run throughout
Nurturing
Keep being useful before, during and after the sale.
Someone who isn’t ready today may be ready later.
Referrals
Someone can recommend a venture without ever becoming a customer.
That’s why referrals aren’t placed only at the end of the customer journey.
The overall principle remains simple:
**Every touchpoint matters.**
The method is the same for Jago, Tiimora and Dumaan.
What changes are the audiences, problems, positioning, offers, channels, actions and signals to measure.

title: We’re building a venture studio
description: Why we’re building a venture studio, how we start with audiences and how we test the first strategies for Jago, Tiimora and Dumaan.
paragraphs: The aim is to launch several ventures in parallel, form hypotheses quickly, build a first version, test it in the market and adjust based on what we observe. Our ambition is simple: **build resilient, profitable businesses.**
Today, we’re working on three ventures in particular.
**Jago** makes it easier to source African products in bulk. We start with shops’ requests and manage the supplier relationship through to the order.
**Tiimora** is operations software for accounting firms, initially focusing on time-consuming tasks around their core accounting work.
**Dumaan** develops frozen West African food products that save time on some preparation steps.
Our ventures usually start with problems we know first-hand, either because we experience them ourselves or because we already work with the people who face them.
So we begin by taking the problem seriously: experience on the ground, existing solutions, alternatives people use today, available information and the people concerned.
Our approach is then fairly simple:
**Understand enough → form a hypothesis → build → test in the real world → adjust.**
We draw mainly on two approaches that resonate with us.

**Seth Godin** has had a strong influence on how I think about marketing: as a generous act of service. Choose a specific audience, understand the change they want, create something that matters to them and earn their trust before trying to sell.
And **Steve Blank**, through Customer Development: discovering and validating needs with customers, treating early convictions as hypotheses to test in the market rather than established truths.
That’s also why we take an **audience first** approach: start with the people we want to serve.
To guide the product, pricing and channels, we first try to understand who we want to serve, which groups we want to test and the difficulties they face.
To structure this initial strategy, we’re currently testing a simple framework: **APOP**.
Audience
Who do we want to serve? Which groups do we want to test? What difficulties do they face?
Positioning
What promise do we want to make to this audience? What benefit do we offer compared with existing alternatives?
Offer
What exactly are we offering, in what form and at what price?
Promotion
How will we bring this offer to market? Through which channels, and with what approach to reaching demand?
We add one final question.
What we want to test
What do we need to observe to consider our hypothesis sound?
**APOP helps us turn what we think we know into an initial strategy we can actually test.**

We’ve done this exercise for **Jago, Tiimora and Dumaan**. Some answers remain hypotheses, particularly the offers, prices and uses we need to test. The articles set out these starting choices; conversations and early trials will help us refine them.
